questions.prompt: Peptide and protein hormones are synthesized in the rough endoplasmic reticulum as preprohormones directed by specific mRNA.
Steroid hormones, such as cortisol and aldosterone, are chemical derivatives of tyrosine.
Antidiuretic hormone (ADH) and oxytocin are synthesized in the cell bodies of hypothalamic neurons rather than in the posterior pituitary gland itself.
Both luteinising hormone (LH) and follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH) belong to the same glycoprotein family and share an identical alpha subunit.
The connecting peptide (C peptide) is packaged and secreted along with insulin in equimolar quantities.
Thyroid hormones circulate in the blood predominantly in the free, unbound form to ensure rapid action on target tissues.
Pancreatic somatostatin is a polypeptide consisting of 14 amino acids that acts to inhibit the secretion of both insulin and glucagon.
Aldosterone is primarily synthesized and secreted by the cells of the zona fasciculata in the adrenal cortex.
Glucagon is produced by the alpha cells of the islets of Langerhans, whereas insulin is produced by the beta cells.
Calcitonin is synthesized and secreted by the parafollicular cells (C cells) of the thyroid gland in response to hypercalcaemia.
Growth hormone-releasing hormone (GHRH) stimulates growth hormone secretion by utilising both the cAMP and IP3/Ca^(2+) second messenger pathways.
Although the thyroid gland secretes more thyroxine (T4), triiodothyronine (T3) is three to four times more biologically active.
Prolactin-inhibiting factor (PIF), which tonically inhibits prolactin secretion, is the catecholamine dopamine.
Oxytocin is a nonapeptide containing nine amino acids.
Secondary adrenocortical insufficiency, caused by ACTH deficiency, is characterized by darkening skin pigmentation.
Human chorionic gonadotropin (HCG) is produced by the placental trophoblast as early as 8 days post-ovulation to rescue the corpus luteum.
Cholesterol is the essential precursor for all adrenocortical steroid hormones.
Positive feedback is the most common physiological mechanism utilized by the body to regulate the secretion of most hormones.
Down-regulation of receptors increases a target tissue's sensitivity to a hormone when blood levels of that hormone are chronically high.
ADH increases water reabsorption in the collecting ducts by directing the insertion of aquaporin-2 channels into the luminal membrane.
Parathyroid hormone  coordinates an increase in serum calcium while simultaneously causing an increase in serum phosphate.
Glucagon increases blood glucose levels by stimulating glycogenolysis in both the liver and skeletal muscle.
Insulin inhibits gluconeogenesis in the liver by increasing the production of fructose 2,6-bisphosphate.
Chronic elevation of TSH levels results in hypertrophy and hyperplasia of the thyroid gland, leading to goitre.
Cortisol plays a permissive role in maintaining normal blood pressure by up-regulating alpha-1 adrenergic receptors on arterioles.
The surge of LH that triggers ovulation at midcycle is the result of negative feedback of estradiol on the anterior pituitary.
Inhibin, synthesized by Sertoli cells in males and granulosa cells in females, inhibits the secretion of FSH from the anterior pituitary.
In the renal collecting ducts, 11-beta-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase converts cortisol to cortisone to prevent it from activating mineralocorticoid receptors.
Hypoglycaemia and starvation are potent physiological stimuli that increase the secretion of growth hormone.
Thyroid hormones increase the basal metabolic rate by inducing the synthesis and increasing the activity of the Na^+/K^+ ATPase.
Prolactin inhibits ovulation by suppressing the synthesis and release of gonadotropin-releasing hormone (GnRH).
PTH directly stimulates renal 1-alpha-hydroxylase to convert 25-hydroxycholecalciferol into the active form 1,25-dihydroxycholecalciferol.
In Graves' disease, circulating TSH levels are typically higher than normal due to lack of feedback inhibition.
A patient with Conn's syndrome (primary hyperaldosteronism) is likely to present with clinical signs of hyperkalemia.
High-dose dexamethasone suppression can be used to distinguish between an ACTH-secreting pituitary tumor and an autonomous adrenal cortical tumor.
Administration of 5-alpha-reductase inhibitors is an effective treatment for benign prostatic hyperplasia by blocking the conversion of testosterone to dihydrotestosterone.
In type II diabetes mellitus, the number of insulin receptors on target tissues is typically increased to compensate for insulin resistance.
A patient with nephrogenic diabetes insipidus will show a significant increase in urine osmolarity after administration of the ADH analogue dDAVP.
During the first trimester of pregnancy, the corpus luteum is the primary source of the progesterone needed to sustain the endometrium.
Factitious hyperthyroidism, caused by the chronic ingestion of exogenous T4, is typically associated with the development of a large goitre.
Spironolactone is a diuretic that acts as a competitive antagonist at the mineralocorticoid receptor, blocking the actions of aldosterone.
Long-term treatment with high doses of glucocorticoids increases the risk of osteoporosis by decreasing bone formation and increasing resorption.
A genetic deficiency of 21-beta-hydroxylase leads to masculinization of female genitalia due to the shunting of steroid precursors into the androgenic pathway.
In chronic renal failure, hypocalcaemia is partially caused by the retention of phosphate, which complexes with ionized calcium in the plasma.
Excess growth hormone secretion in an adult after epiphyseal closure results in a significant increase in femur length and overall height.
Progesterone maintains pregnancy by increasing the uterine threshold to contractile stimuli, thereby keeping the myometrium quiescent.
In patients with primary adrenocortical insufficiency (Addison disease), the Na^+:K^+ molar ratio in the plasma is characteristically increased.
Vitamin D deficiency in adults leads to the clinical condition known as rickets.
An acute increase in extracellular pH (alkalemia) results in an increase in the plasma concentration of free, ionized calcium.
In a patient with 17-alpha-hydroxylase deficiency, the excessive production of DOC and corticosterone results in a secondary increase in renin and aldosterone secretion.
